chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee' from Zarif ibn Nasih from Thalabah ibn Maymun from 'Abdullah ibn Yazid, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the leper and the leper with skin disease (pox), do they lead the Muslims in prayer? He said, 'Yes.' I said, 'Does Allah test the believer through them?' He said, 'Yes, and has Allah not written trials only for the believers?'
This is applicable in a state of necessity; but when there is the ability to find others like them, they are not to be led in prayer in any case.
And it is permissible that this report includes a group whose characteristics are like those of these two; in that case, it is permissible for them to lead the people in prayer in any case.
And the restricted one does not lead the unrestricted, nor does the one with paralysis lead the healthy. This was narrated.

key_terms.الْأَبْرَصِ: Person with pox or skin disease
key_terms.الْمَجْذُومِ: Person with leprosy or skin disease
key_terms.الْمُطْلَقِينَ: The unrestricted (those without that specific defect)

ai.seo_question: Can a person with leprosy or physical disability lead congregational prayer in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes that physical ailments like leprosy or pox do not disqualify one from leading congregational prayer, affirming that such conditions are specific trials for believers. However, scholarly interpretation distinguishes between necessity and preference, noting that while they may lead, they are not preferred over those without defects, nor does a person with a specific limitation lead those who are free from it. This ruling underscores the principle that spiritual authority in prayer is not diminished by bodily imperfection, provided the individual is otherwise qualified.
